It has three or four strings, and it is played kneeling with the body standing on the floor, sounding when the horsehair bow is drawn across the strings. A beginner can first tune it like a shamisen, commonly hon-chōshi or san-sagari, then practise holding the bow and turning the body to change strings. The bow hair is not drawn tight and can be removed; the bow stick can usually be taken apart into two pieces at the middle.

It once formed the sankyoku ensemble with the koto and the shamisen, and it is also used in jiuta, sōkyoku, gidayū, kabuki, folk song and religious performance; the source mentions "Semi no Uta" (composed by Yoshizawa Kengyō), "Kōan-kin", "Tsuru no Sugomori", "Chidori no Kyoku" and "Etchū Owara-bushi". It also appears in jazz and blues, played solo by Eric Golub or in John Kaizan Neptune's cross-cultural jazz group.

The kokyu is Japan's only traditional bowed string instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs classification 321.312-7, a chordophone. Its form is like a scaled-down shamisen, and on the Japanese mainland the body is mostly square while the Okinawan variant, the kūchō, has a rounder body; it usually has three strings, and four are also found, and it is played with the body upright and the horsehair bow drawn across the strings. The kokyu was an important member of the sankyoku ensemble, alongside the koto and the shamisen, and it also appears in jiuta, sōkyoku, gidayū, kabuki, folk songs and religious works; in the early period it was mostly passed down by blind musicians.
胡弓為日本唯一傳統弓弦樂器，起源未有定論，與東南亞弓弦樂器相近，經印尼、馬來西亞: The kokyu is Japan's only traditional bowed string instrument. Its origin is not settled: it resembles the bowed strings of Southeast Asia, came to Okinawa by way of the rebab of Indonesia and Malaysia, and was later used on the Japanese mainland. It first appears in documents in the early Edo period, slightly later than the shamisen, and it was passed down by blind musicians at the same time as jiuta and sōkyoku. In the middle of the Edo period a kokyu repertoire took shape, divided into the Osaka, Kyoto and Nagoya schools, and the instrument was used in the sankyoku ensemble, gidayū-bushi, kabuki and folk song. In the late Meiji period Miyagi Michio improved the large kokyu; from the Meiji period into the twentieth century it was gradually replaced by the shakuachi in sankyoku, and later the four-string version widened its range and made it more widespread, and it entered jazz and blues.
胡弓琴身多與三味線類似，日本本土琴身常用花梨木，蒙貓皮或狗皮；琴杆現多用紅木、紫: The kokyu's body is mostly similar to the shamisen's, and on the Japanese mainland it is often of rosewood covered with cat or dog skin; the neck is now usually of a wood such as padauk, rosewood or karaki. The sounding body is mainly the strings, generally silk. The bow stick may be rosewood, karaki or bamboo, sometimes lacquered; the hair is a cylindrical hank of horsehair. The Ryukyuan kokyu's body may be of ebony and other materials, with a bowl-shaped soundbox that in the past was made from a coconut shell and covered with snakeskin. The materials of the other parts are not stated.
胡弓音色深沉而富有表現力，呈現出溫潤、幽玄的音質，常帶有略微沙啞的質感。其音域主: The kokyu's timbre is deep and expressive, with a warm, mysterious quality that often has a slightly husky texture. Its range is centred on the lower middle register; the high notes sound sharp and dramatic, the low ones full and bleak. The instrument uses a resonating box, and the friction of the bow hair on the strings produces a continuous sound which the box makes more penetrating and distant. Compared with the bright splendour of the Western violin the kokyu is more inward and profound; it is close to the Chinese erhu but lacks the erhu's sharpness and has more softness and nimbleness. Its timbre particularly suits inward feelings such as grief and longing, and it is a distinctive instrument of traditional Japanese music.
